nameStory: This tiny algae gets its sweet name from its striking resemblance to watermelon flesh - bright pink to red coloring that stands out dramatically against white snow. The red color comes from astaxanthin, a protective pigment that helps the algae survive in harsh, freezing conditions where most other life can't exist.
description: Watermelon snow isn't actually a plant, but a fascinating cold-loving algae that turns snow fields brilliant pink or red during summer months. This microscopic green algae contains special red pigments that create colorful patches across snow surfaces. You'll see it as areas of pink, red, or even blood-red coloration on otherwise white snow, most commonly in high mountain areas where snow persists through summer.

idTips.label: Color when compressed
idTips.description: Step on suspicious pink snow or make a snowball - it will turn much more intensely red when compressed, almost like squeezing juice from fruit

idTips.label: Summer snow patches
idTips.description: Look for it only on snow that persists through summer months, typically in shaded areas or high elevations where winter snow lingers

idTips.label: Pink to red coloration
idTips.description: Appears as patches of pink, rose, or deep red coloring on white snow - the intensity can vary from barely noticeable to dramatically bright

idTips.label: Stains clothing and boots
idTips.description: Walking through it leaves bright red stains on shoe soles and pink marks on pants cuffs that are quite noticeable

idTips.label: No odor
idTips.description: Unlike what you might expect from colored snow, watermelon snow has no particular smell - it's odorless

habitat: In New England, you'd most likely encounter this rare phenomenon on the highest peaks during late spring or early summer, where snow patches persist in shaded areas or north-facing slopes. Look for it on mountains like Mount Washington in New Hampshire, where elevation and weather conditions allow snow to linger well into the warmer months.

seasonality.spring: Most likely time to spot watermelon snow as temperatures warm but snow patches remain, especially in late spring when melting begins in earnest.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation when the contrast between melting snow and red algae is most dramatic, particularly in persistently cold, high-elevation areas.
seasonality.fall: Extremely rare to find, as most snow has melted by this time except in the most protected, highest elevation spots.
seasonality.winter: Not visible during winter months when the algae is dormant and buried under fresh white snow.

funFact: Walking through watermelon snow will literally stain your boots and pants bright red, as if you've been stomping through berry juice - and this colorful algae actually speeds up glacier melting by darkening the snow surface and absorbing more heat from the sun!
confusionNotes: The main confusion is thinking something is wrong or contaminated when you first see pink or red snow. Remember: if it gets redder when you compress it and has no smell, it's likely this harmless algae, not pollution or animal blood.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'watermelon snow,' this organism is actually a type of green algae - the red color you see comes from protective pigments, while the green chlorophyll is still there underneath. It's completely harmless to touch, though some sources suggest not eating it in large quantities.
compareHints: As the only Chlamydomonas species documented in New England, watermelon snow is unique in our region. Other snow algae exist worldwide but create different colors - some produce green or orange tints. The key distinguishing feature is the intense red color that appears when the snow is compressed, which is specific to this astaxanthin-rich species.
